Task and constraints: You are given an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a given stock on the i^th day. The method returns the requested result for the stated inputs.
Idea: Tracks two buy states and two sell states as prices arrive, updating the best profit for one and then two transactions.
Technique and why it applies: State compression keeps only the best values for the four transaction stages.
Invariant: Each state is the best achievable balance/profit at its stage after processing prices so far.
Edge cases: The initial negative-infinity buy states prevent a buy from being assumed before a price; no more than two transactions are represented.
Complexity: The author labels O(n) time and O(1) space, matching one pass and four scalar states.

Task and constraints: You are given an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a given stock on the i^th day. The method returns the requested result for the stated inputs.
Idea: Maintains best buy and sell states for each allowed transaction count. For each price it updates the best purchase using the previous sale state and then updates the best sale.
Technique and why it applies: Dynamic programming compresses the at-most-k transaction states into arrays.
Invariant: buy[j] is the best balance after buying for transaction j; sell[j] is the best profit after selling up to j transactions.
Edge cases: At most two transactions are permitted here; empty input returns zero through initial sell values. Update order determines whether the current price is used consistently.
Complexity: The author labels O(k*n) time and O(k) space; with k=2 this is linear time and constant-size state.

Task and constraints: You are given an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a given stock on the i^th day. The method returns the requested result for the stated inputs.
Idea: Builds best one-transaction profits for every prefix, builds best profits for every suffix, then tests every split by adding the two values.
Technique and why it applies: Prefix/suffix decomposition combines at most one transaction on each side of a split.
Invariant: The prefix array stores best profit ending no later than each index; the suffix array stores best profit starting no earlier than it.
Edge cases: A single transaction or no profitable trade yields zero. insert(0, ...) in the reverse pass shifts the list each time and is costly.
Complexity: The author labels O(n) time and O(n) space, but repeated insert(0, value) makes the reverse pass O(n^2) time in Python; arrays use O(n) space.

Task and constraints: A phrase is a palindrome if, after converting all uppercase letters into lowercase letters and removing all non-alphanumeric characters, it reads the same forward and backward. Alphanumeric characters include letters and numbers. The method returns the requested result for the stated inputs.
Idea: Builds a new lowercase string by concatenating each alphanumeric character, then compares it with its reverse.
Technique and why it applies: Filtering and normalization reduce the input to the characters that must be compared for palindrome symmetry.
Invariant: cleaned contains exactly the alphanumeric characters processed so far, in lowercase and original order.
Edge cases: Punctuation and spaces are ignored; an empty cleaned string is a palindrome. Repeated string concatenation can copy the accumulated string repeatedly.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Worst-case time and space can be O(n^2) time due to repeated concatenation, and O(n) stored string data.

Task and constraints: A phrase is a palindrome if, after converting all uppercase letters into lowercase letters and removing all non-alphanumeric characters, it reads the same forward and backward. Alphanumeric characters include letters and numbers. The method returns the requested result for the stated inputs.
Idea: Uses two pointers from both ends, skipping non-alphanumeric characters and comparing lowercase forms of the next valid characters.
Technique and why it applies: Two pointers compare mirrored characters without building a cleaned copy.
Invariant: All valid characters outside the current interval have already matched their counterparts.
Edge cases: Punctuation-only strings return true; Unicode alphanumeric characters follow Python's isalnum/lower behavior.
Complexity: The author labels O(n) time and O(1) space, consistent with scanning inward and constant state.

Task and constraints: A transformation sequence from word beginWord to word endWord using a dictionary wordList is a sequence of words beginWord -> s1 -> s2 -> ... -> sk such that: The method returns the requested result for the stated inputs.
Idea: Builds wildcard-pattern adjacency for words, performs breadth-first search to record all parents at the shortest distance, then recursively walks the parent tree to construct ladders.
Technique and why it applies: BFS finds shortest levels while retaining multiple parents; DFS reconstructs all shortest paths.
Invariant: The parent map records predecessors from the preceding BFS level, and nodes are finalized by level.
Edge cases: If endWord is absent, the method returns []; multiple shortest parents must be preserved. The number of output paths can be exponential.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. BFS cost depends on word count and length; DFS/output cost is proportional to all returned paths, and parent/output storage can be large.

Task and constraints: A transformation sequence from word beginWord to word endWord using a dictionary wordList is a sequence of words beginWord -> s1 -> s2 -> ... -> sk such that: The method returns the requested result for the stated inputs.
Idea: BFS explores one transformation level at a time, generates one-character substitutions using wildcard patterns or letters, and returns when endWord is reached.
Technique and why it applies: Breadth-first search finds the shortest sequence because each edge represents one character change.
Invariant: The queue/frontier contains words at the current distance and used prevents revisiting them.
Edge cases: If endWord is not in the dictionary, variants explicitly return zero/empty; removing visited words prevents cycles.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Complexity depends on dictionary size, word length and alphabet; BFS stores visited words/frontier, while ladder-II variants also store parent links and output paths.

Task and constraints: A transformation sequence from word beginWord to word endWord using a dictionary wordList is a sequence of words beginWord -> s1 -> s2 -> ... -> sk such that: The method returns the requested result for the stated inputs.
Idea: Runs bidirectional BFS from beginWord and endWord, expanding the smaller frontier and recording directed links for later path reconstruction.
Technique and why it applies: Bidirectional BFS reduces the search frontier, while the link graph preserves shortest routes.
Invariant: left/right are the current frontiers; tree edges are oriented according to is_reversed to support reconstruction.
Edge cases: endWord must be in the dictionary or the code returns []; many shortest paths can make output exponential.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Search is reduced by bidirectional BFS, but worst-case work and memory depend on dictionary size and all returned paths.

Task and constraints: Given an unsorted array of integers nums, return the length of the longest consecutive elements sequence. The method returns the requested result for the stated inputs.
Idea: Converts nums to a set, then starts a forward scan only at values with no predecessor and counts consecutive set members.
Technique and why it applies: Hash-set start detection prevents rescanning every sequence from its interior values.
Invariant: Each run is counted from its smallest value, identified by the absence of i-1.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero; duplicates disappear in the set. Expected set membership is constant time.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Expected time and auxiliary space are O(n); each value is visited in a start scan and in one sequence count.

Task and constraints: Given an unsorted array of integers nums, return the length of the longest consecutive elements sequence. The method returns the requested result for the stated inputs.
Idea: Initializes a dictionary of boundary lengths and, for each value not already processed, combines the consecutive-run lengths immediately left and right to update the run's endpoints.
Technique and why it applies: Hash-map boundary lengths merge adjacent consecutive sequences without sorting.
Invariant: The stored lengths at run boundaries represent the length of the consecutive interval ending/starting there.
Edge cases: The code initializes result to 1, so empty input incorrectly returns 1 even though the statement permits an empty array. Duplicate values are skipped after their length is set.
Complexity: The author labels O(n) time and O(n) space, matching dictionary access and storage.

Task and constraints: Given a string s, partition s such that every substring of the partition is a palindrome. Return all possible palindrome partitioning of s. The method returns the requested result for the stated inputs.
Idea: Uses memoization on substrings. For each center it expands odd and even palindromes, combines partitions of the prefix and suffix, and deduplicates completed partitions with a set of tuples.
Technique and why it applies: Center expansion detects palindromes, while recursive partition combination enumerates all valid cuts.
Invariant: lookup[s] caches all palindrome partitions for substring s, and result_set prevents duplicate partition lists within a call.
Edge cases: Single-character strings have one partition; repeated characters can produce many partitions. Slicing and tuple conversion allocate copies, and the cache can grow substantially.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Runtime is output- and substring-dependent and can be exponential; memoized results and recursive substring copies require substantial space.

Task and constraints: Given a string s, partition s such that every substring of the partition is a palindrome. The method returns the requested result for the stated inputs.
Idea: Precomputes which substrings are palindromes from right to left, and for each start index minimizes cuts by trying every palindromic ending position.
Technique and why it applies: Dynamic programming separates palindrome recognition from the minimum-cut recurrence.
Invariant: lookup[i][j] records palindrome status; mincut[i] is the minimum cuts needed for suffix s[i:].
Edge cases: A one-character string returns zero; the empty-string case is outside the stated constraints. The inner test accesses smaller substring states already computed.
Complexity: The author labels O(n^2) time and O(n^2) space, matching the palindrome table and two nested loops.

Task and constraints: There are n gas stations along a circular route, where the amount of gas at the i^th station is gas[i]. The method returns the requested result for the stated inputs.
Idea: Builds gas-minus-cost deltas, duplicates the circular sequence, uses a running maximum-subarray-style scan to choose a candidate start, then verifies that one full circuit never has negative fuel.
Technique and why it applies: Prefix-sum/greedy candidate selection reduces possible starts; a final pass verifies feasibility.
Invariant: The verification sum tracks fuel change along the candidate route and must stay nonnegative.
Edge cases: A valid unique start is guaranteed when a solution exists. Duplicating deltas allocates a second array, and maxi defaults to zero if no positive running sum appears.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Time is O(n) and space O(n) because deltas is duplicated, unlike the constant-space alternative.

Task and constraints: There are n gas stations along a circular route, where the amount of gas at the i^th station is gas[i]. The method returns the requested result for the stated inputs.
Idea: Tracks total gas balance and current segment balance. When the current balance becomes negative, it sets the next station as the candidate and resets the segment sum.
Technique and why it applies: Greedy elimination proves any start inside a failed segment cannot complete the circuit.
Invariant: current_sum is the balance since the current candidate; total_sum is the overall circuit balance.
Edge cases: If total balance is negative it returns -1; otherwise the last reset position is a valid start under the problem's uniqueness guarantee.
Complexity: The author labels O(n) time and O(1) space, matching one pass and scalar sums.

Task and constraints: There are n children standing in a line. Each child is assigned a rating value given in the integer array ratings. The method returns the requested result for the stated inputs.
Idea: Starts each child with one candy, scans left-to-right to give increasing ratings one more than the previous child, then scans right-to-left to repair descending-rating constraints and sums the allocation.
Technique and why it applies: Two directional passes enforce each child's comparison with both neighbors.
Invariant: The first pass satisfies rising runs; the reverse pass raises a child when its rating exceeds the right neighbor and its candy count is not already larger.
Edge cases: Equal ratings impose no strict inequality. Single-child input needs one candy; the array of counts uses linear storage.
Complexity: The author labels O(n) time and O(n) space when supplied; both passes are linear and temp/candies stores one count per child.
